recipes.name: Maple-Brined Pork Loin
ingredients_raw: salt and freshly ground black pepper

steps.text: Make the brine: Mix water, maple syrup, salt, garlic, ginger, black pepper rosemary, and red pepper flakes together in a large stainless steel bowl.
Start the pork: Place pork loin in brine, cover, and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, or up to 10 hours at most.
Remove pork from brine; discard brine. Pat pork dry and season all over with salt and black pepper.
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C).
Heat vegetable oil in an oven-proof skillet over high heat. Add pork and turn to brown on all sides, about 10 minutes total.
Transfer the skillet to the preheated oven and roast until pork is browned, about 40 minutes.

Mix maple syrup and Dijon together in a small bowl; spread mixture all over top and sides of roast. Continue to cook until pork is slightly pink in the center, about 15 more minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should read at least 145 degrees F (63 degrees C).

raw_recipe.headline: Maple-Brined Pork Loin
raw_recipe.description: Chef John's easy maple syrup brine for boneless pork loin works its magic overnight to keep the meat moist and add a sweet hint of maple flavor.

review.reviewBody: Excellent flavor! Make sure that you don't over cook your roast - I put the glaze on at internal temp of 135 and next time I would do that at 125 - and cook to not quite 145. You want the FINAL temp. to be 145, after resting. This is company worthy and very easy. Enjoy!

I wanted to make this with a pork loin roast as the recipe suggests but at the butcher's those roasts were small and looked to be lacking in any fat at all ( to me that means tasteless), so I opted for a tied boneless pork blade roast that was 3.5 lbs and nicely marbled. I made the brine as described in the recipe but increased the ingredients by half to accommodate the larger roast. I also added 3/4 tsp of liquid smoke to the brine and I'm glad I did. You have to be stingy with liquid smoke...too much and it dominates but in this case it was a nice underpinning for the maple flavour. The blade roast rendered its fat and was so lovely and moist without being the leas bit greasy. I took it out of the oven to glaze when it was 125ºF, then returned it to the oven for another 15 minutes. Next time, I will cook it at this stage to 145ºF on the meat thermometer since the slices were a wee bit pink in the middle but the ends were fine. I made extra dijon-maple syrup glaze and fellow diners spooned it liberally over meat and green beans - and loved it also. I rounded out the feast with mashed potatoes and cumin-maple roasted pepper squash. Great meal. Thanks, Chef John.

I thought the maple-dijon glaze was amazing; I will definitely use that again. But I really don't think 10 hours is long enough to brine a 2 1/2 pound loin. I could not taste that brine in the meat at all. If I try this again, I will brine it overnight.

WHAM-O! This is the recipe that makes the saying, "...would make shoe leather taste good" a reality. I would trust this recipe to a very expensive or large piece of pork to, even something as special as a crown roast! It was especially great when made in a pressure cooker ( how I made it for Easter) I was pleasantly surprised with not only how tasty the meat was but how easy it was to make once I got the brine done. I cannot say enough good about it. 
If you want to make it exceptional, go the extra mile and buy real maple syrup. You will be rewarded!!!

Husband, "THAT is the best pork I have EVER had in my whole life!" That says it all. My hubby John had bought a 4 pound pork loin, thawed it out, and was wondering how on earth could he prepare it other than the same boring way we've been doing for 30+ years of married life.
I came across this recipe and thought, "Heck, I'll give it a try!" Mind you I've never brined a thing in my life. 
So, I followed the recipe except DOUBLED the amounts as this was a larger hunk of pork. 

**Used 1/4 tsp Chili Powder in place of 1 Tsp Red Chili Flakes 
**Used 1/4th tsp of Ground Ginger for every 1 TBSP of Chopped Ginger.
**Soaked the loin for 2 days and it was perfect!
After removing loin from oven it was cut into slices and put back in the juices. Oh, boy! 
**The only thing I will do differently next time is cut the salt by half. It left me very dehydrated the night we ate the loin. Other than that it was utterly fabulous!!!

I had been trying to crack the mystery of making pork roast that is both flavourful and moist for a long time. My go-to has been to wrap the roast in bacon, which works well - but I really wanted to try something different.
This recipe was it; so simple and so full of flavour.
The only change I made was extending the brining time to 14 hours, and upping the oven to 350, which the times given worked perfectly for.
I also cooked the roast on a bed of baby carrots, onions, garlic, fresh oregano, and thyme. I added a cup of sherry to the left-over glaze mixture, a couple of pats of butter, and poured it in with the vegetables, which I roasted for another hour.
I tried a bite of the pork once it had rested for 15 minutes and it was bursting with flavour and full of juices - definitely the moistest pork I have ever cooked!
I will be trying brine again soon, and experimenting with different seasonings and liquids. Chef John scores again!!!

Delicious! I used a pork loin that I’d had in the freezer for awhile. I figured if this didn’t turn out well, it would be my fault for using a roast that had been frozen for too long. But, it was so tender and flavorful. I had to use ground ginger for the brine because I didn’t have fresh. That was the only change I made. I had enough of the sliced pork left over, so I poured water into the iron frying pan and scraped the bits that included the glaze from the meat. I loaded the slices and the juice into a container for freezing. Looking forward to leftovers!
I made a pan sauce while the roast was resting. I deglazed the pan with 1/2 cup chicken broth, reduced down a few minutes. Remove from heat and swirl in 1 tablespoon butter. Fantastic!

Everyone raved about this - the pork was so juicy. I altered very little. Seasoned more before browning with extra spices to our liking, and doubled the maple syrup and mustard, keeping half of it to add to to the drippings to make a gravy. Delicious!

Used brown sugar and maple flavoring instead, so delicious, forgot glaze but cooked at 225 for 2 hours approx i had a 8 # roast to do
nice way to cook pork nice and tender....Esq
Good but not fabulous. But easy to do, and a good way to use pork loin if you don't have tenderloin.
I adapted this for loin chops, turned out great and really loved the flavors.
We all agreed this was the BEST Pork Loin Roast EVER! Very simple to make. Served with a Sauteed Apple sauce.

This brine is perfect just as stated in the recipe with no adjustment. I did find it works with dry ginger or a herb other than rosemary if those ingredients are not available. The pork loin could be cooked by smoking or another means besides oven roasting. But I like the crispiness and flavors achieved by browning in a cast iron

I love Chef John’s recipes and humor. I really wanted to enjoy this meal. I didn’t deviate from the recipe. It was not as flavorful as his molasses- brined pork chop recipe. I used a meat thermometer and took it out of the oven @ 135.

I usually make tenderloin, but my butcher was out, and all they had was a pork loin roast. I had never made this before. Obviously, I did not have time to brine my 4.5 lbs roast for 8 hours, but the 4 hours were plenty. I grilled for an hour, and it was super moist. I did pat dry the roast about 30 minutes before grilling and added a simple pork rub, but the texture was really what stood out. I made 7 people very happy!
